whyCorrect: Track what each study is evidence for. The wastewater study found no correlation, which prompted the hypothesis that the carbon-mercury association exists only in undisturbed water. Tjerngren then studied water disturbed by urban development and found the association anyway, so a second kind of human disturbance did not erase it. That defeats the sweeping hypothesis and leaves only the narrower conclusion that the wastewater result describes wastewater, not human disturbance in general.

whyWrong.A: The passage is about whether a correlation is present, not about how high the levels of carbon or mercury are; no measured amounts are ever compared between the two kinds of disturbed water.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text mentions measurement methods, and inventing a methodological difference would explain away Tjerngren's finding rather than follow from it.
whyWrong.D: How many bodies of water each type of disturbance affects is never discussed and would not bear on whether the two substances are correlated.

commonMistakes: Treating the wastewater study as the finding to be explained, when the sentence beginning with However signals that Tjerngren's result is what the conclusion must follow from.

whyCorrect: The research findings describe how people react to seeing red: they associate it with power and dominance, and past experience with red objects makes them cautious and hesitant. Manchester United wears red at home, so it is the opposing players who see red, not United's own players. Caution and hesitation in opponents means worse play from them, which fits the club's strong home record.

whyWrong.A: The findings describe how observers respond to red, not how wearing red makes the wearer feel; excitement is never mentioned.
whyWrong.C: This reverses who wears red. If red signals dominance, it is Manchester United that would look more dominant, not their opponents.
whyWrong.D: The caution and hesitation belong to the people confronted with red. Saying United played less skillfully also contradicts the fact that they won more than half their home matches.

tips: When a passage ends with a claim about one team's uniform, ask who is looking at that uniform before deciding whose behavior changes.

whyCorrect: Strip the interrupting comparison and the sentence is Luxembourg's constitution _____ as the 9th shortest in the world. The subject is the singular noun constitution, and everything between the commas, including the plural word words, is a modifier that cannot supply the subject. A singular present-tense verb is ranks.

whyWrong.A: Rank is the plural present-tense form and does not agree with the singular subject constitution.
whyWrong.B: Are ranking is plural, and the progressive also misstates a fixed ranking as something in progress.
whyWrong.D: Have ranked is plural, so it disagrees with constitution regardless of tense.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearest noun, words or Canada's, act as the subject instead of the real subject far to the left.

whyCorrect: The main clause is Suetonius's book, Pratum, is a lost work. Between the subject and its verb sits the relative clause no copies of which _____, and a relative clause built on which needs a real conjugated verb of its own. Survived supplies it, so the clause reads no copies of which survived and the sentence stays complete.

whyWrong.A: Having survived is a participial form with no tense-carrying verb, so the which clause never becomes a clause.
whyWrong.B: To survive is an infinitive, which likewise leaves the which clause without a finite verb.
whyWrong.D: Surviving is a present participle and produces the same fragment; which demands a conjugated verb, not a participle.

tips: Whenever you see which or of which, look for the conjugated verb that belongs to it before you choose.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete general claim, and everything after it is a three-part list of examples that spells that claim out. A colon is the mark that introduces an explanation or list after a complete statement. The items in that list are long and already contain their own commas, which is why they are separated from one another by semicolons.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon here would fold the general claim into the list itself, making it read as the first of four parallel items rather than the statement the examples illustrate.
whyWrong.B: A comma joins two complete sentences, producing a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all the two complete statements run together.

commonMistakes: Assuming that because the rest of the sentence uses semicolons, the first break must be a semicolon too.

whyCorrect: The phrase is dendrochronologist Valerie Trouet, a job title used as part of the name, exactly like historian Jane Smith. A title that identifies which person is meant attaches directly to the name with no punctuation between them. Adding any mark would cut the name loose from the title that identifies her.

whyWrong.A: The comma splits the title from the name it modifies, as though Valerie Trouet were a separate item.
whyWrong.B: A dash signals a break or an interruption, but there is no break between a title and the name that follows it.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete statement and introduce what comes next; claims dendrochronologist is not a complete statement.

tips: If the title answers which one, it is part of the name and takes no punctuation.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has a complete main clause: the member nations share a commitment to collective defense. What follows the comma is a second unit beginning each NATO member, and a comma cannot join two complete sentences. Pledging keeps that unit a modifying phrase describing how the commitment works, so the comma is legal.

whyWrong.A: Has pledged is a conjugated verb, so each NATO member has pledged is a complete sentence and the comma becomes a splice.
whyWrong.C: Pledges is likewise conjugated and creates the same comma splice.
whyWrong.D: Is pledging is a conjugated verb phrase, not a participle on its own, so it also produces two complete sentences joined by a comma.

commonMistakes: Choosing by tense or agreement when the real question is whether the second half is allowed to be a sentence at all.

whyCorrect: The relative clause is a lens that illuminates how and why people make particular choices, and illuminates is already its verb. The blank sits inside a phrase fenced off by commas immediately after that, so it cannot be a second verb for the same subject. Combining turns the fenced-off phrase into a modifier and the sentence holds together.

whyWrong.A: Combines gives the single relative pronoun that two conjugated verbs, combines and illuminates, with no conjunction between them.
whyWrong.B: Combine has the same double-verb problem and is also plural, clashing with the singular lens.
whyWrong.D: Is combining is a conjugated verb phrase, so it too leaves the clause with two verbs.

tips: Read past the commas to find the clause's real verb before deciding whether the blank can be a verb.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a cause: Italian was the default language of opera scores for centuries. The second gives the effect that follows for singers now, who must read Italian markings in eighteenth-century scores. A result transition is what links those two, and Thus is the only one offered.

whyWrong.A: However sets up a contrast, but the second sentence agrees with the first rather than complicating it.
whyWrong.C: Lastly closes a sequence of listed items, and no such list is running.
whyWrong.D: Granted concedes a point to an opposing argument; no opposing argument has been raised.

tips: Ask whether the second sentence follows from the first or pushes against it before scanning the choices.

whyCorrect: The dates settle it. The first sentence is set in 1965, and the second names strips syndicated in 1994 and 1996. The transition has to move the reader forward in time, which is what Later does.

whyWrong.A: That is introduces a restatement, but the second sentence adds new strips and new dates rather than rephrasing the first.
whyWrong.B: Previously reverses the chronology; 1994 and 1996 come after 1965, not before it.
whyWrong.C: For example would make the later strips instances of the claim about Wee Pals, but Wee Pals was the first, so the others cannot be examples of it.

commonMistakes: Reaching for For example because the sentence names specific titles, without checking that they illustrate the previous claim.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim about Belew's detailed costume design as seen in the whole jumpsuit. The second narrows to one feature of that same suit, its blue rhinestones, as evidence for the same claim. In particular is the transition that zooms from a whole to a telling detail.

whyWrong.A: Next implies a step in a sequence of events, but the two sentences describe the same garment, not two stages.
whyWrong.C: Soon marks a passage of time, and no time has passed between the sentences.
whyWrong.D: Nevertheless signals a contrast, but the rhinestones confirm the claim about attention to detail rather than complicating it.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to emphasize a similarity, so the sentence must name both trails and say something true of each. The notes give one shared property: both are rail trails. B states exactly that and nothing else.

whyWrong.A: This describes only one path, in Maine, so no comparison is made at all.
whyWrong.C: Whereas signals a contrast, so this emphasizes a difference in location rather than a similarity.
whyWrong.D: This gives only the Simon Kenton Trail's description and never mentions the Papermill Trail.

tips: When the goal says similarity, cross out any choice that names only one item or uses a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for a reason, so the sentence has to state a benefit and tie it back to nautical miles. The notes supply the chain: a nautical mile equals one minute of latitude, latitude and longitude account for Earth's curvature, and mariners use those coordinates to calculate quickly. C links all three into a because statement about why nautical miles are used.

whyWrong.A: This defines a nautical mile and mentions charts but never says why that makes nautical miles useful, so it describes rather than explains.
whyWrong.B: The subject here is nautical charts against flat maps; nautical miles are never explained at all.
whyWrong.D: This contradicts the notes, which say that measuring with latitude and longitude coordinates does account for Earth's curvature.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice that uses the most notes instead of the one that answers the why.

whyCorrect: The goal is a similarity between the two named refuges, so the sentence must cover both and state something shared. Only D puts Bear Valley and Ellicott Slough together under one common purpose, protecting endangered species, which is the shared category the notes set up.

whyWrong.A: This mentions only Bear Valley and reports a fact about the national total, so the second refuge never enters the comparison.
whyWrong.B: While signals a contrast, and acreage is the one point on which the notes make the two refuges differ.
whyWrong.C: This names only Ellicott Slough, so it presents no comparison between the two refuges.

tips: A similarity sentence needs both subjects and a shared predicate; anything with only one subject is out immediately.

whyCorrect: The end of the sentence tells you what the blank must mean: the fossil reveals important details about the time in which LH 4 lived. A word for shedding light on a period is illuminate. It also parallels identify in the not only, but also structure, since both describe what the remains let researchers learn.

whyWrong.A: Substitute means to put one thing in place of another, but the fossil is not replacing the Pliocene epoch.
whyWrong.B: Imitate means to copy, which makes no sense as something a fossil does to a geological period.
whyWrong.D: Design means to plan or create, and nothing can create an epoch that has already passed.

whyCorrect: Compare the data with the rule that follows. Desai and colleagues found that strong democratic institutions tend to hold inflation down, yet Belgium, with strong institutions, had the higher rate. The blank needs a word meaning departing from the expected pattern, which is anomalous.

whyWrong.A: Inexplicable means impossible to explain, which overstates the case; the result is unexpected, not beyond explanation.
whyWrong.B: Unfounded means lacking any basis, a word for a claim rather than for a measured inflation rate.
whyWrong.C: Facetious means joking or not meant seriously, which cannot describe a statistical result.

commonMistakes: Reading however as a signal that the result is wrong, when it signals only that the result runs against the general tendency.

whyCorrect: The sentence says no amount of justification will persuade these particular drivers, so their belief has to be one that rules out any increase in advance. If they already regard the current toll as excessively high, no argument for a higher one can reach them. Exorbitant carries exactly that sense of a price far beyond what is reasonable.

whyWrong.A: Contentious describes a dispute surrounding the toll, not a judgment about its amount, so it gives no reason those drivers would be unpersuadable.
whyWrong.C: Warranted means justified, which describes drivers who approve of the current toll, and approval of the existing charge gives no ground for refusing to hear a case for raising it.
whyWrong.D: Equivocal means open to more than one interpretation, which cannot describe a fixed dollar amount.

tips: The blank has to explain the resistance stated earlier in the sentence, not just describe the toll.

whyCorrect: The colon means the words after it define the blank. What follows is that over a long study a substantial number of participants withdraw or lose contact. The single word for that steady loss of participants is attrition, and it explains why a study must recruit far more people than it needs at the end.

whyWrong.B: Circumspection means caution in one's conduct and says nothing about losing participants.
whyWrong.C: Impartiality means freedom from bias, which is a quality of the researchers rather than a reason to enroll extra people.
whyWrong.D: Replicability is whether another team could repeat the study, which the text after the colon never touches.

whyCorrect: The blank is set against traditional forms that stay recognizable even as they change. The contrasting forms borrow from fables and narratives at once and straddle the line between prose and poetry, so their defining trait is having no fixed shape. Amorphous means exactly that, lacking a definite form.

whyWrong.A: Neutral means taking no side, which does not describe a form's shape or its mixing of genres.
whyWrong.B: Customary means usual or traditional, the opposite of the unconventional forms the sentence is describing.
whyWrong.D: Dispersed means scattered across space, which does not apply to the structure of a literary form.

commonMistakes: Missing the while at the start of the sentence, which sets up a contrast the blank must complete.

whyCorrect: The first sentence is only setup: The Times says the English ideal is that everyone do as he likes. The word But turns to what the passage is actually there to assert, that culture works to move people toward a sense of what is beautiful and to make them like it. The purpose of the whole text is that claim about what culture does.

whyWrong.A: Arnold gestures at what is indeed beautiful, but he never argues the fact-versus-opinion point; his subject is the effect culture has on people.
whyWrong.B: The English appear only as the occasion for the argument, and no analysis of a distinctively English taste follows.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the passage tracks change over time; the contrast is between two views held at once, not between an earlier and a later view.

tips: When a short passage turns on But, the main purpose almost always lives in the half after the turn.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports two favorable outside views: the laity think Mr. Ely remarkably able, and his fellow clergy think him discreet and agreeable. The second sentence switches to what he actually does, avoiding warm discussion, withholding his own opinions, and never letting anyone laugh at him. Those habits are precisely what keeps the good opinion intact, so the structure is other people's view followed by the conduct that sustains it.

whyWrong.A: No change in anyone's view is recounted; the opinions described stay steady throughout.
whyWrong.B: London is mentioned only as a place the townspeople imagine him impressing, and the passage never compares his neighbors' judgment with a Londoner's or explains any deception.
whyWrong.D: The passage shows his guardedness but never states his private behavior or gives a motive for concealing himself.

whyCorrect: Follow the experiment to its conclusion. Goldfish steered a wheeled tank across land to a pink board, and Givon concludes from that success that their navigational skills are not tied to water. The main idea is that fish can navigate outside water when a machine gives them the means, which is what A says.

whyWrong.B: This states the opposite of the researchers' conclusion; the whole point is that the skill was not confined to water.
whyWrong.C: The treats are one detail of the setup, and the passage is about navigation in fish, not about reward training in animals generally.
whyWrong.D: This is the hypothesis the experiment undercuts, since the fish navigated in an environment that was not their own.

whyCorrect: The last sentence states the author's position directly: rather than being an arbitrary stylistic choice, the modified voice is a commentary on how digital technology shapes human experience. A statement that the practice is merely aesthetic and carries little social meaning is the exact position that sentence rejects. So A is the one the author would disagree with.

whyWrong.B: Commenting on technology is not the same as counteracting it, and the passage never credits hyperpop with offsetting anything, so there is no claim here for the author to contradict.
whyWrong.C: The passage describes the music as commenting on a wider condition, not as shaping listeners' self-understanding, so this is unsupported rather than something the author argues against.
whyWrong.D: This restates the author's own conclusion, so it is the statement the author would most agree with.

commonMistakes: Hunting for the choice that is merely unsupported instead of the one the text explicitly rules out.

whyCorrect: The passage has two halves joined by But. The first says Nixon is most famous for Watergate; the second says his legacy is complex and names achievements on tribal sovereignty and health care reform. The main idea has to hold both halves together, which is that the scandal he is known for obscures real accomplishments.

whyWrong.A: Magruder and Woods appear only as examples of the people involved in the scandal; the passage never says they are the source of his reputation.
whyWrong.B: The link to the Affordable Care Act is one supporting detail from the second half and leaves out the Watergate half entirely.
whyWrong.C: This elevates two names mentioned in passing into the point of the passage.

tips: A main-idea answer must account for both sides of a passage that pivots on But.

whyCorrect: The claim is about how devotedly and carefully the father usually tends the lawn, so the quotation has to show habitual, meticulous effort. B gives both: shaving the lawn as if it were a priest's chin is an image of exacting care, and working at it all season in the evenings after supper establishes that the care is routine.

whyWrong.A: This shows the father searching for the damaged flower and noticing Jim, which is about the accident, not about how he tends the lawn.
whyWrong.C: This is a quiet scene-setting moment after the mower stops; it describes the surroundings rather than the father's dedication.
whyWrong.D: This follows Jim across the lawn and mentions the machine in passing, but it says nothing about the quality or regularity of the father's work.

tips: Match the quotation to every part of the claim, including words like typically that require evidence of a habit.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: the speaker states an intention, and the art is meant to appeal universally and across generations. B is a declaration of intent, Let me make the songs for the people, and it names both age groups, old and young, plus wherever they are sung. No other option states an intention and a span of ages.

whyWrong.A: This describes what the weary world needs; it is a diagnosis rather than a statement of what the speaker intends to make.
whyWrong.C: This is a blessing on a nation, which is a specific patriotic subject rather than an intention to reach everyone.
whyWrong.D: This is a private recollection of the speaker's mother and says nothing about the audience for her art.

whyCorrect: The claim is not just that she refuses John but that she urges him to look elsewhere instead of waiting on her. B does exactly that: she names Meg and Moll as women who might accept him and tells him plainly not to remain single for her sake. The other quotations refuse him without ever pointing him toward someone else.

whyWrong.A: This denies that she ever loved him and complains about his pestering, but it never suggests he look elsewhere.
whyWrong.C: This offers friendship in place of love, which is a refusal rather than encouragement to pursue another relationship.
whyWrong.D: This sets the terms of a friendship and warns him off hidden hopes, but it still does not send him toward anyone else.

whyCorrect: Combine the two pieces the passage gives you. The hypothesis is that a New York Spanish dialect has formed partly through contact with English, and the prior research says younger speakers of a nonmajority language borrow from the majority language more than older speakers do. Since English is the majority language here, younger Spanish speakers would be doing more of the borrowing that creates the dialect, so they should show the dialect more than older speakers do.

whyWrong.B: The cited research contrasts younger with older speakers, not one kind of neighborhood with another, so nothing supports a claim about multilingual neighborhoods.
whyWrong.C: This is a prediction about future growth in languages and dialects that neither the hypothesis nor the research addresses.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the research, which is about borrowing from the majority language, English, not from other nonmajority languages.

commonMistakes: Adding a variable the passage never measured, such as neighborhood or time, instead of using the one it does supply, speaker age.

whyCorrect: The archaeologists' assumption gives you a test: a demographic shift that breaks the handing down of expertise shows up as several specialized crafts declining at once. At the Alazani sites only gold filigree drops around 1500 BCE, while copper-alloy metallurgy and most other crafts keep flourishing. The signature of a population disruption is therefore missing, so whatever ended the filigree work happened without a break in the population passing down skills.

whyWrong.B: The evidence here is a single craft declining while others continue, which never puts the assumption about simultaneous declines to the test.
whyWrong.C: This says goldsmithing continued, contradicting the steep drop in filigree objects, and it also asserts demographic shifts the evidence does not establish.
whyWrong.D: The passage says copper-alloy metallurgy continued to flourish, not that it expanded, and cross-cultural transmission is never mentioned.

tips: When a passage states an assumption in the form if X then Y, check whether Y actually appears in the evidence before concluding X.

whyCorrect: The opening question has already been asked, and the blank is the answer to it, followed by a sentence that supplies more detail about Spenser. An answer is a statement, so it needs statement word order, subject before verb, and a period at the end. Only it was invented by an author does both.

whyWrong.A: The word order is correct for a statement, but the question mark turns it into a question the passage has no reason to ask a second time.
whyWrong.C: Was it inverts subject and verb, which makes a question, yet it ends with a period.
whyWrong.D: Wasn't it is likewise question word order punctuated as a statement.

commonMistakes: Assuming that because the passage opened with a question, the blank must be a question too.

whyCorrect: The subject is the word robot, a single word, so the verb must be singular. The sentence reports something that happened in 1920, so it must be past tense. Was is the only singular past form on the list.

whyWrong.A: Were is the plural past form and does not agree with the singular subject.
whyWrong.B: Were being is plural and its progressive aspect wrongly presents a single first use as ongoing.
whyWrong.D: Have been is plural and present perfect, which clashes both in number and with the fixed date 1920.

tips: A word named in quotation marks is one thing, however many things it refers to.

whyCorrect: Read past the long dash-enclosed aside and the main clause is astronomers deduced that the fluctuation was caused by an exoplanet. Deduced is already the verb for astronomers, so the blank cannot supply a second one. Perceiving makes the opening a modifying phrase that says how the astronomers came to that deduction.

whyWrong.A: Perceived is a conjugated verb, leaving astronomers with two verbs, perceived and deduced, and no conjunction between them.
whyWrong.B: Had perceived creates the same double-verb problem, with a tense shift on top of it.
whyWrong.C: Were perceiving is a conjugated verb phrase, so the sentence still has two competing verbs.

commonMistakes: Losing track of the main verb because a long parenthetical sits between the blank and it.

whyCorrect: Neither noun in the blank owns anything. You place your hands, so hands is a plain plural object, and the hands go between the two antennas, another plain plural. Apostrophes mark possession, not more than one, so both words stay apostrophe-free.

whyWrong.A: Hand's and antenna's are singular possessives, but nothing is possessed and the sentence already says two antennas and later your hands.
whyWrong.C: Both words carry plural possessive apostrophes, and neither noun possesses anything in the sentence.
whyWrong.D: Hands' is a plural possessive, which would need a following noun naming what the hands own; there is none.

tips: Before adding an apostrophe, name the thing being owned. If you cannot, leave it off.

whyCorrect: The blank sits between the verb is and its complement, just 66.7 degrees Fahrenheit. A verb and the word that completes it are one unit, and Standard English does not put a mark of punctuation inside that unit. No punctuation is correct.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two complete sentences, and just 66.7 degrees Fahrenheit is not a sentence.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete statement, but the average summer temperature is stops mid-thought.
whyWrong.D: The comma needlessly separates the linking verb from the value it introduces.

commonMistakes: Adding a pause where you would take a breath aloud; punctuation follows structure, not breathing.

whyCorrect: The sentence states a permanent fact of chemistry, which English puts in the simple present, and the surrounding sentences use the present as well. The subject a calcium atom is singular, so the form is has.

whyWrong.A: Is having is progressive, and have in the sense of possessing does not take the progressive; it also clashes with the timeless nature of the fact.
whyWrong.B: Had puts a fact that is always true into the past.
whyWrong.C: Has had suggests a state that began earlier and may have ended, which misrepresents a fixed property of the element.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general rule: sleeker vehicles are more aerodynamic than bulkier ones. The second sentence supplies a specific case of that rule, the streamlined Cessna against the boxy semitruck. Moving from a rule to a specific case is what for example marks.

whyWrong.A: However would signal that the Cessna complicates the rule, but it obeys the rule exactly.
whyWrong.C: Additionally adds a separate point, whereas this sentence illustrates the point already made.
whyWrong.D: Meanwhile marks two things happening at the same time, and no time relation is at issue.

commonMistakes: Choosing however because the sentence contains a contrast; the contrast is between the jet and the truck inside the example, not between the two sentences.

whyCorrect: The clause before the semicolon says what is not true, that Chaucer did not write in Modern English. The clause after supplies the correction, that he wrote Middle English. Rather is the transition that replaces a denied statement with the accurate one.

whyWrong.B: As a result claims the second clause is caused by the first, but writing Middle English is not a consequence of not writing Modern English; it is the same fact stated positively.
whyWrong.C: Similarly points to a parallel case, and only one writer's language is under discussion.
whyWrong.D: Finally closes a sequence, and no sequence of steps has been running.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives Taylor's goal, keeping stations like KBFT thriving, and the third gives the action she took to reach it, founding a support network. The action follows from the goal, so the transition has to show consequence. Hence is the only one that does.

whyWrong.A: In reality corrects a mistaken impression, and nothing before it has been presented as a misconception.
whyWrong.C: By contrast sets two things against each other, but founding the organization matches her stated aim rather than opposing it.
whyWrong.D: In other words restates the previous sentence, while this one reports a new event.

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing to emphasize: where Somalia stands in the world. That is the note saying it has the sixth-largest under-fifteen population globally, and B is the only choice that states it. The percentage it adds is supporting detail, not a substitute for the rank.

whyWrong.A: This invents a causal link between Somalia's youth population and Africa's that the notes never make, and it states no rank.
whyWrong.C: The subject here is Africa's share and the UN's comment, so Somalia's standing in the world never appears.
whyWrong.D: This is about the condition the UN attaches to Africa's growth and says nothing about Somalia at all.

tips: Rank means a position in an ordered list, so look for an ordinal like sixth-largest rather than a percentage.

whyCorrect: Duration means how long the relationship has lasted, so the sentence needs a starting point tied to the present. A gives the pairing a start date of 1990 and the word since, which measures the stretch of time from then to now.

whyWrong.B: This locates Borovichi in Russia and glosses the term twin town; no length of time appears.
whyWrong.C: This compares their partnership to other sister cities' and mentions distance, neither of which is duration.
whyWrong.D: Since the end of World War II describes when the sister city concept developed in general, not when these two cities paired, so it misapplies a date from a different note.

commonMistakes: Taking any choice containing a date as an answer about duration; the date has to belong to the relationship being measured.

whyCorrect: The goal names one subject, Sirius A, so the sentence has to be about that star and give its mass. D reports the figure of 2.063 solar masses and, by noting that one solar mass equals the Sun's, makes the number mean something. The other three never state Sirius A's mass.

whyWrong.A: This defines the unit and names Proxima Centauri, so Sirius A never appears.
whyWrong.B: This is pure definition of solar masses with no star's mass given.
whyWrong.C: This compares the Sun with Proxima Centauri, a different star from the one the goal names.

whyCorrect: Similarly tells you the second sentence repeats the pattern of the first, where Crain incorporated Choctaw hymn elements into folk-pop. The blank therefore needs a word for combining two musical traditions into one work. Blended is that word, and the construction blended X with Y fits it exactly.

whyWrong.A: Confused means mistaking one thing for another, which describes an error rather than a deliberate artistic combination.
whyWrong.B: Compared means examining two things side by side, not merging them into a single piece of music.
whyWrong.D: Replaced would mean Latin pop drove out the Afro-Indigenous music, contradicting the idea of combining styles.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis was that a sudden shift to arid conditions caused the kangaroo extinctions. The new evidence shows the climate change came well before the extinctions, which breaks the timing the hypothesis depends on. A hypothesis whose evidence no longer fits has to be changed, so paleontologists are forced to revise it.

whyWrong.B: Interpret means to work out what something means, but the hypothesis is already clear; what the new dates require is a change to it.
whyWrong.C: Recollect means to remember, and the problem is not that the hypothesis was forgotten.
whyWrong.D: Introduce would mean putting the hypothesis forward for the first time, but it was already proposed in the previous sentence.

whyCorrect: The sentence stresses range, from a plaza sculpture to a street mural, and calls it an array of works. What such variety does for art lovers is meet their appetite fully. Satiate means to satisfy an appetite completely, which is what an array of works does to a taste for art.

whyWrong.A: Supplant means to take the place of something, so it would say the artworks replace people's tastes rather than fulfill them.
whyWrong.B: Mitigate means to make something less severe, which would oddly mean the art reduces people's taste for art.
whyWrong.C: Venerate means to regard with deep respect, which is something people do toward art, not something art does to tastes.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes the museum as a large collection, and the second sends visitors outdoors for more art on top of it. The blank names what the street works do to the museum visit: add to it. Supplement means to add something extra to what already exists.

whyWrong.A: Mitigate means to lessen, which would say the street art reduces the experience.
whyWrong.B: Satisfy would suggest the museum visit left a need unmet, but the text presents the outdoor works as an addition, not a fix; you also satisfy a desire, not an experience.
whyWrong.C: Provoke means to trigger a reaction, which does not describe extending an experience the visitor is already having.

commonMistakes: Choosing a positive-sounding word without checking that it fits the noun after the blank.

whyCorrect: While sets Whistler against his contemporaries, whose approach was sentimental, so the blank must name the opposite of sentimental. The next sentence confirms it by linking him to photographs that seem to be objective documentation of life. An eye that keeps emotion out is dispassionate.

whyWrong.A: Tranquil means calm or peaceful, which describes a mood in the scene rather than the absence of sentiment in the artist's viewpoint.
whyWrong.B: Peculiar means odd or distinctive, which does not oppose sentimental and does not fit the comparison to objective documentation.
whyWrong.C: Nostalgic is a form of sentimentality, so it would make Whistler resemble his contemporaries instead of contrasting with them.

whyCorrect: The first half establishes what the Highwaymen's paintings have in common, repeated compositional structures and subjects such as breaking waves and backcountry pines. But then turns to individuation, and Sam Newton's more realistic style is the example that proves it. So the structure is shared framework, then a claim of individual variation backed by a case.

whyWrong.B: The passage never reports a common perception that the work is derivative, and the Newton example works against that reading rather than reinforcing it.
whyWrong.C: No historical explanation of why the group shared a style is given, and nothing is said about members turning to unconventional themes.
whyWrong.D: The passage does not describe how the collective formed or claim that any member was especially influential on the others.

whyCorrect: Each half of the passage supplies a reason juvenilia matter to scholars. The first says unpublished work by later-famous authors reveals their artistic development; the second says recovering work by lesser-known writers such as Ashford is essential to understanding literary history. The purpose that covers both halves is presenting why scholars find juvenilia valuable.

whyWrong.A: Publication difficulties are never discussed; Dickens's poem is simply described as unpublished and Ashford's novels as published.
whyWrong.C: The passage compares two scholarly interests in juvenilia, not the achievements of young writers against those of adults.
whyWrong.D: Ashford and Dickens are examples of two research emphases, and no claim is made that one writer's work has more merit.

tips: When a passage has two halves joined by But, check whether they conflict or both support one larger point before picking a purpose.

whyCorrect: The text gives you one rule and two body masses. Baleen whales eat up to about 30% of their mass per day, the minke tops out near 4,000 kg, and the fin whale reaches 80,000 kg and eats as much as 24,000 kg of krill daily. A far heavier whale eating a comparable share of its own mass must take in far more krill, so the fin whale out-eats the minke.

whyWrong.A: A minke whale of at most 4,000 kg cannot eat 24,000 kg of anything in a day; that figure belongs to the fin whale alone.
whyWrong.B: The passage never mentions competition for food or any shortage facing minke whales.
whyWrong.D: The first sentence says all baleen whales feed on krill this way, so there is no difference in whether krill is in the diet, only in how much.

commonMistakes: Attaching the 24,000 kg figure to both whales because it appears at the end of a sentence that names both.

whyCorrect: The researchers' chain is specific: items are moved, the shopper hunts for them, the hunt takes her past products she would not otherwise pass, and she buys something unplanned. A reproduces every link, since the cleaning supplies were not in their usual spot, the search led past a notebook, and the notebook was an unplanned purchase.

whyWrong.B: This shopper searched but bought less than planned, so it shows the inconvenience of a moved item without the extra purchase the explanation predicts.
whyWrong.C: A mailed coupon is an obvious external cue of the kind the passage contrasts with layout changes, and the purchase was the one the shopper came for.
whyWrong.D: This is about choosing a larger store, with no rearrangement and no unplanned purchase.

tips: A support question wants every step of the stated mechanism, not just the outcome.

whyCorrect: The claim is that Didion shows a dark underside to an era usually remembered for peace and love, so the quotation has to put that darkness on the page. A is a catalog of it: bankruptcies, public auctions, routine killings, missing children, abandoned homes, vandalism. Nothing else on the list makes the darkness that concrete.

whyWrong.B: This describes a mood of disappointed expectation, with steady markets and high social purpose; it reports that hopes went unmet without showing what the darker reality consisted of.
whyWrong.C: This is scene-setting about arriving in San Francisco and making friends, and carries no dark content at all.
whyWrong.D: This depicts drifting adolescents and is bleak in tone, but it characterizes one group of young people rather than establishing the darker condition of the period as a whole.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts that must both appear: harsh conditions, and a change in the soldiers' shared mood. C supplies both, since the beating sun is the condition and it dulls their minds and bodies until they fall silent, which is the mood of the whole group changing.

whyWrong.A: This is landscape description of the sierra and fog, with no soldiers and no mood.
whyWrong.B: This reports the soldiers' route and lack of rest, which is strenuous, but says nothing about how they felt.
whyWrong.D: This describes the terrain they crossed all day; the hills are bleak, but the soldiers' state of mind is never mentioned.

whyCorrect: The claim is about where Aunt Sue's stories come from. A says it outright: she never got them out of any book, they came right out of her own life. That is a direct statement of personal experience as the source.

whyWrong.B: This describes how the characters seem to merge into her voice as she tells the stories, which is about the telling, not the origin.
whyWrong.C: This is an image of dark shadows moving through the stories and says nothing about where they came from.
whyWrong.D: This gives the setting in which the stories are told, not their source.

whyCorrect: The reason for the skepticism has to be the flaw the passage just described. The meta-analysis sets 176 individuals as the minimum needed before a population-level handedness finding can be separated from statistical noise, and the 1991 chimpanzee study used 14. Fourteen is an order of magnitude short of that threshold, so its finding cannot be distinguished from noise.

whyWrong.A: This assumes the conclusion, that chimpanzees are not really right-handed. The meta-analysis says nothing about how common the trait is, only about how many individuals you must examine.
whyWrong.B: No difference in how the two studies defined or measured handedness is mentioned anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: The sentence is about why the 1991 claim of right-handedness is doubtful, and criticizing the gorilla study's size would not bear on that claim.

whyCorrect: Line up the two findings with the host counts. Three-host parasites, which need at least two vertebrate species, declined as sea temperatures rose; two-host parasites, which need only one vertebrate, held steady. Since vertebrates are the hosts most vulnerable to climate change, the natural reading is that warming hit vertebrate populations in ways that knocked back the parasites depending on several of them, while whatever happened to the single vertebrate host of the two-host parasites left their numbers alone.

whyWrong.A: This has the direction backwards, since C. parophrysi is the two-host parasite whose abundance was largely stable, so it was the less affected of the two.
whyWrong.B: If the fish were largely unaffected by warming, nothing in the study would explain why three-host parasite abundance fell as temperatures rose.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the relationship. Depending on more vertebrate species went with greater decline, so sensitivity rises with the number of vertebrate hosts rather than falling with it.

commonMistakes: Reading a choice that uses the right vocabulary, such as correlated and vertebrate species, without checking which way the relationship runs.

whyCorrect: The main clause is emulsifiers are compounds that serve to stabilize an emulsion, and it already has its subject and verb. The opening phrase must therefore be a modifier describing emulsifiers, and emulsifiers are the things being used, not the things doing the using. The past participle Used gives the passive sense the sentence needs.

whyWrong.A: Using is active, so it would say the emulsifiers use something in food and cleaning products, reversing the relationship.
whyWrong.B: To use states a purpose and leaves a dangling infinitive with no one performing the action.
whyWrong.C: They are used is a complete sentence, so joining it to the main clause with only a comma creates a splice.

tips: Decide whether the noun after the comma does the action or receives it; that choice is between the -ing and the -ed participle.

whyCorrect: The passage explains how the cooperative model works as a permanent arrangement, and every other verb around the blank is present tense: is, stands, are shared. A general truth stated in the present takes the simple present, and the plural subject the workers takes benefit.

whyWrong.B: Had benefited is past perfect, which places the benefit before some earlier past moment the passage never establishes.
whyWrong.C: Benefited puts a still-true feature of the model into the past.
whyWrong.D: Were benefiting is past progressive, which frames an ongoing general fact as something that was happening during a finished stretch of time.

tips: Match the blank to the tense of the verbs already in the passage before considering anything else.

whyCorrect: Cover the long phrase set off by commas and the sentence is Oscar James Dunn _____ his term as lieutenant governor in 1868. The subject has no verb yet, so the blank must supply a conjugated one. Began is the only finite verb offered.

whyWrong.A: To begin is an infinitive and leaves the sentence a fragment with a subject but no verb.
whyWrong.B: Having begun is a participial phrase, so the sentence still never reaches a main verb.
whyWrong.C: Beginning is a participle and produces the same fragment.

commonMistakes: Reading the long appositive as if it contained the sentence's verb; nothing inside those commas can serve as the main verb.

whyCorrect: The pronoun in the blank stands in for the artworks named in the main clause, which is plural. It is also the subject of debuted and must be a pronoun that can take a plural verb. They is the only plural personal pronoun offered.

whyWrong.B: That is singular and, used as a bare subject, points to no clear thing.
whyWrong.C: It is singular and cannot stand for the plural artworks.
whyWrong.D: This is singular as well, so it disagrees with the noun it refers to.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is already a complete sentence about astronomers detecting a phenomenon. Everything after it, the explosion of a massive star with its two appositives, is a long noun phrase that names what the phenomenon was; it has no verb of its own. A colon is the mark that follows a complete statement and introduces the identification that explains it.

whyWrong.A: A period demands a complete sentence after it, but The explosion of a massive star, also known as a supernova, an extremely bright yet transient event has no verb.
whyWrong.B: It was the produces two complete sentences joined by only a comma, which is a splice.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon also requires a complete sentence on each side, and the material after it is a noun phrase.

tips: Before choosing a semicolon or period, check that what follows has a subject and a verb of its own.

whyCorrect: The passage opens with Where, so the blank must finish an actual question, and the sentences after it answer that question. An English question formed with a question word needs the auxiliary before the subject, did the word come from, and it ends with a question mark.

whyWrong.A: There is no auxiliary, so come is left unconjugated, and the period marks it as a statement.
whyWrong.B: The word did come from keeps statement order after Where, which is not how a direct question is formed.
whyWrong.D: The word order is right for a question, but the period contradicts it.

whyCorrect: Cuba is offered as a place where the Spanish legacy is still audible, and Sardinia is offered as a place where it is not. The sentence with the blank is a general statement, a former colony's tie can be so tenuous, that then names one example. Sometimes is what makes that statement true of certain cases rather than of former colonies as a class, which is exactly the qualification the Sardinia example supports.

whyWrong.B: On the other hand would set the whole class of former colonies against Cuba, asserting as a rule what the sentence itself presents as only one example.
whyWrong.C: At the same time also frames the second claim as an across-the-board counterweight rather than an occasional case.
whyWrong.D: In addition signals another instance of the same pattern, but Sardinia is the opposite of the Cuba pattern, not more of it.

commonMistakes: Grabbing a contrast transition because the two cases differ, without checking whether the sentence is a general rule or an occasional case.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says Baku's tower is one of many outright replicas of the Eiffel Tower. The second widens the point to structures that are not replicas but still echo the design. That is another piece of evidence for the same idea, so an additive transition is what is needed.

whyWrong.A: On the contrary corrects a previous statement, but the second sentence extends the first rather than denying it.
whyWrong.B: Consequently claims the Lyon tower exists because of the Baku replica, a causal link the text never makes.
whyWrong.C: Invariably would claim that every such tower does this without exception, which the hedge though not exact replicas contradicts.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the rule: internationally popular demonstration sports were treated differently from regionally popular ones, which got a single showcase. The second sentence shows that rule playing out, with handball becoming a medal event and kaatsen appearing only in 1928. The transition has to say that the specific outcomes follow the pattern just described, which is what Accordingly does.

whyWrong.A: Moreover introduces a further, separate point, but this sentence supplies the details of the point already made.
whyWrong.C: Granted concedes something to an opposing view, and no opposing view is in play.
whyWrong.D: However signals that the second sentence pushes against the first, yet the handball and kaatsen cases confirm it. The contrast in that sentence is between the two sports, not between the two sentences.

tips: Locate what the contrast word inside a sentence is contrasting before assuming the sentence contrasts with the one before it.

whyCorrect: To emphasize a similarity the sentence has to name both films and state something that is true of each. D does that twice over: both would be valuable records of their era, and both are lost. The notes support every piece of it.

whyWrong.A: This pairs each film with a different director, so it lists two separate facts instead of a shared trait.
whyWrong.B: The subject here is film archives, and neither of the two movies is mentioned.
whyWrong.C: Only The Fighting Ranger appears, so there is nothing for it to be similar to.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for one thing, the setting of the story. Only one note gives a place, that it takes place in Harlem, and A is the choice that reports it.

whyWrong.B: This names the author, which is who wrote it rather than where it is set.
whyWrong.C: This gives the book it appeared in, which is where it was published, not where the story happens.
whyWrong.D: This describes the narration, which is how the story is told rather than where.

tips: Answer only the goal as stated; a true sentence about the wrong fact is still wrong.

whyCorrect: An advantage means a benefit and the feature that produces it, so the sentence has to link a trait of Oak Tree House to what it did for the people there. The notes say it was built under a rock overhang and that the overhanging ledges kept off heavy rain and snow. D states both halves and connects them with Since.

whyWrong.A: This asserts that the location was an advantage without ever saying what the advantage was.
whyWrong.B: This gives the region and the dates of habitation, neither of which is a benefit.
whyWrong.C: The flat terrain and the large terraced buildings belong to Yucca House, so this attributes another site's feature to Oak Tree House.

commonMistakes: Accepting a sentence that uses the word advantage as though naming the concept were the same as explaining it.

whyCorrect: The not only, but also structure makes the blank parallel to illuminate, so it must name something the fossil lets researchers do with knowledge. What they do with steps in hominid evolution is make them out from the evidence. Discern means to perceive or distinguish something that is not obvious, which fits both the parallel and the object.

whyWrong.A: Exploit means to use something for advantage, and researchers do not put evolutionary steps to use.
whyWrong.B: Yield means to produce or give up, so it would make the paleoanthropologists the source of the steps rather than their observers.
whyWrong.C: Prioritize means to rank in order of importance, which is not what a fossil helps researchers do with a sequence of evolutionary changes.

whyCorrect: The data were stranded on obsolete storage and the transfer project is making them available again. The blank names the effect of that on their usefulness: the data can be used once more, as the mention of lunar geology confirms. Renewing captures bringing back something that had lapsed.

whyWrong.A: Persisting means continuing to exist, but the sentence needs an action taken on the data's usefulness, and persisting cannot take that object.
whyWrong.B: Installing means putting equipment in place, which describes hardware rather than the value of a data set.
whyWrong.D: Exceeding would mean surpassing the data's usefulness, but a project cannot go beyond a quality it is restoring.

whyCorrect: The sentence turns on a time and a place: at seven the husband was not there, so his wife explains that a meeting kept him. Appeared here means showing up in person at the expected hour, which is arrived. The excuse about being detained confirms it, since being detained is what prevents someone from getting somewhere.

whyWrong.A: Pretended is a sense of appear used with a following to be or as if, and there is no such construction here.
whyWrong.B: Developed fits appear when something comes into existence, such as a symptom, not when a person shows up.
whyWrong.C: Responded would require something to respond to, and the sentence gives only a time.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says these theaters prefer pleasing audiences to taking risks. The second sets a safe choice, a classic they are eager to produce, against a risky one, an unknown playwright's work. The blank has to be the opposite of eager, so it must express reluctance.

whyWrong.A: Determined would make them keen to stage the risky work, which reverses the preference the passage establishes.
whyWrong.C: Fortunate describes good luck rather than an attitude toward a decision, and it does not oppose eager.
whyWrong.D: Surprised describes a reaction to something unexpected, not a reluctance to take a risk.

whyCorrect: The dinosaurs are extinct, so their breathing cannot be observed directly. Birds have the same air sacs and hollow bone extensions, so paleontologists study birds to learn about the dinosaurs. A thing studied in place of something unavailable is a proxy for it.

whyWrong.A: A harbinger announces something still to come, but the dinosaurs came long before the birds.
whyWrong.B: An emissary is a person sent to represent someone in dealings with others, which does not describe one body system standing in for another in research.
whyWrong.D: Subordinates would rank bird respiratory systems below the dinosaurs' in some hierarchy, and the passage draws an equivalence rather than a ranking.

tips: When a passage says a living thing is studied because an extinct one cannot be, the blank usually names a stand-in.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences set up a problem, that consumer devices claim to measure VO2 max but their accuracy is unproven. The third sentence answers it with the Cambridge model, which tracks heart rate more accurately and monitors fitness changes. The passage exists to bring that new model forward as a better option.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the accuracy of current devices is unproven, which is not the same as proving them inaccurate; nothing here demonstrates anything.
whyWrong.C: No advice to consumers is given, and the passage in fact points toward a tracker rather than away from trackers in general.
whyWrong.D: No findings from the new model are reported, and the text never says when or whether it will reach the public.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that describes only the setup sentences and ignores the sentence the passage builds toward.

whyCorrect: Two sentences report the mouse finding, that gut microbes seem to drive the urge to run, and the last sentence extends it, postulating that a pill could give people the same motivation. The passage does not stop at the mice; it uses them to raise a possibility for humans. That extension is the purpose.

whyWrong.A: Understanding mice is what the researchers did, but the text keeps going, so this leaves out the point the passage ends on.
whyWrong.C: This asserts the research will be used to help people, while the text only postulates that it could.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the passage claims motivation is beyond a person's control; the pill idea implies the opposite.

whyCorrect: The last sentence answers the question directly: Miguel hoped not only to meet the sisters but to make the acquaintance of the poet himself. The two things he wanted are an introduction to the Ureña girls and an introduction to their father, which is what D reports.

whyWrong.A: It is the narrator, not Miguel, who says she had learned everything Alejandro could teach; Miguel is not the tutor's student.
whyWrong.B: Miguel is described as an aspiring poet, but the passage never says he lacked instruction or that he wanted the father as a mentor.
whyWrong.C: No reading or discussion of Miguel's own poems is mentioned anywhere in the text.

tips: When a question asks why, look for the sentence that states a character's hope or intention rather than inferring from their description.

whyCorrect: Every clause pairs a strength with the excess it avoids: daring but not rash, prompt but not thoughtless, firm but not harsh. The passage then reports the result, respect from his officers and love from his comrades. Taken together the text says the qualities he brings fit the job he is doing.

whyWrong.B: The passage credits him with kindness and devotion to the men he drills, not with any effort to win notice.
whyWrong.C: His superiors are said to respect him, so there is no conflict between serving his comrades and being appreciated above.
whyWrong.D: No mistakes appear in the text; each phrase names a fault he does not have.

whyCorrect: The claim has two conditions: the soldiers are at a distance, and the town itself is what strikes them. C satisfies both, since Juchipila rises in the distance, white and sunlit against forest and mountain. That is the town seen from afar and described in admiring terms.

whyWrong.A: This describes the canyon hills the soldiers crossed and calls them dirty and bald, so neither the town nor a striking impression appears.
whyWrong.B: Here the soldiers are already inside the streets, so the town is no longer being viewed from afar.
whyWrong.D: This is a description of the sierra and its fog, not of Juchipila.

whyCorrect: The claim is about the road itself and about a distant place. C says the Dixie Pike grew from a goat path in Africa, which ties this Georgia road directly to another continent. That is the connection the claim describes.

whyWrong.A: This tracks southern soil carried north to Washington, so the subject is the wind and the soil rather than the road.
whyWrong.B: This describes a repair gang arriving along the railroad track and mentions no distant place.
whyWrong.D: This reports only what the road is called.

whyCorrect: The claim needs both parts: something new in irrigation practice, and a measurable gain in efficiency from it. D supplies both, since sprinkler systems were developed in response to water scarcity and the share of national water use going to irrigation fell as a result, well below the world figure. That is an innovation with an efficiency payoff.

whyWrong.A: This compares humidity across regions of California and explains where irrigation is needed, saying nothing about innovation or efficiency.
whyWrong.B: This argues that greater efficiency would be valuable, which is a statement of what is desirable rather than evidence that innovation has delivered it.
whyWrong.C: This shows an ancient design still in use, which speaks to durability rather than to efficiency increasing over time.

commonMistakes: Accepting a quotation that merely contains the word efficiency instead of one that shows efficiency actually rising.

whyCorrect: The passage concedes the autobiographical parallels but insists that much of the novel is pure invention. Readers who look only for matches between the book and Ballard's life will treat the invented material as if it were reported. What they miss is the inventing itself, so they fail to see how much of the book is Ballard's creation.

whyWrong.A: How many people read the novel is never at issue; the passage is about how it is read.
whyWrong.B: No other writers are mentioned, so influence from earlier authors cannot be what these readers overemphasize.
whyWrong.D: These readers do the opposite, since their error is insisting on real-life sources for everything in the book.

whyCorrect: Translate each grain type into an environment. Most of the sediment is fine mudstone, which settles slowly out of still or slow-moving water, so a standing body of water was there for a long time. Those fine layers show cracks from episodic drying, so the water body dried out now and then, and the occasional coarse sandstone intervals mean flowing water, that is streams, at times. B is the only option that keeps the lake dominant and long-lived while allowing both the drying and the streams.

whyWrong.A: This rules out a lake, but the mudstone that makes up most of the section is exactly what a standing body of water leaves behind.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the proportions, giving the streams the long span and the lake a brief one, while the evidence says fine lake sediment dominates.
whyWrong.D: The desiccation cracks are in the fine-grained lake sediment, so it is the lake that dried episodically, not just the streams.

tips: In these inference items each piece of physical evidence maps to one clause of the answer; check that every clause has evidence behind it.

whyCorrect: Look at what comes after the blank: separate borders of neighboring countries, modeled a vision of the EU's unifying aims. Modeled has to be a verb for the course, so the words before it must form a phrase, not another verb. And, crossing separate borders of neighboring countries, gives the sentence two verbs for its subject, was and modeled, with a participial phrase tucked between commas.

whyWrong.A: The comma after and cuts the verb crossed off from the conjunction, and it still leaves modeled with nothing to attach to.
whyWrong.B: Had crossed makes a second verb and then strands modeled as a third verb with only a comma before it.
whyWrong.C: Crossed produces the same problem: the sentence reaches modeled with two verbs already used and no conjunction left.

commonMistakes: Choosing a parallel-looking verb without reading to the end of the sentence, where a second verb is already waiting.

whyCorrect: The subject of the when clause is a given industry, singular, and the blank must refer back to that same industry. So the pronoun has to be singular and the verb has to match it. It often consists is the only pairing that does both.

whyWrong.A: They is plural and has no plural noun to point to; water and electricity are examples inside a dash-enclosed aside, not the subject.
whyWrong.B: This is a demonstrative with no clear referent, and using it here makes the sentence point vaguely at a situation rather than at the industry.
whyWrong.C: These is plural, so it disagrees with a given industry.

tips: Material inside dashes is an aside; the pronoun after it still refers to the noun the sentence was already about.

whyCorrect: The verb before the blank is were projected, and project in this sense is completed by an infinitive: someone is projected to do something. The blank therefore takes to gain, which then leads into the number of new jobs.

whyWrong.A: Are gaining is a conjugated verb phrase, so the sentence would have two verbs in a row with no connector, and its present tense clashes with the 2019 to 2029 projection.
whyWrong.C: Had gained is also conjugated and puts a forecast about the future into the past perfect.
whyWrong.D: Gains is a conjugated singular verb, which cannot follow were projected and does not agree with lawyers anyway.

whyCorrect: The clause many travelers recommend is doing identifying work: it tells you which European city out of many is meant. An identifying clause is not fenced off with a comma, and it is introduced by that. So the blank is city that with no punctuation.

whyWrong.A: That does not follow a comma in Standard English; a comma calls for which.
whyWrong.B: The comma makes the clause an aside, which would say that the city is being merely described rather than picked out of the many European cities the word one implies.
whyWrong.C: In which, garbles the structure and drops the object recommend needs, and the comma after which is not permissible.

whyCorrect: The second sentence has a subject, She, and an object, them, but no verb until the blank fills it. Only a conjugated verb can serve, and the subject is singular with the surrounding text in the present tense, so weaves is correct.

whyWrong.A: Weaving is a participle, leaving She typically weaving them a fragment.
whyWrong.C: To weave is an infinitive and cannot be the main verb of a sentence.
whyWrong.D: To be weaving is likewise an infinitive form and produces the same fragment.

whyCorrect: The subject is The Proto-Atlantic-Congo language, one language. Everything between it and the blank, the phrase naming it the common ancestor of 1,453 African languages, is a modifier, and the plural noun languages inside that modifier is not the subject. A singular subject in the present takes is.

whyWrong.A: Were is plural and past, so it disagrees in number and shifts the tense away from the present-tense claim that follows.
whyWrong.C: Are is plural, matching the nearby languages rather than the actual subject.
whyWrong.D: Have been is plural as well, and the present perfect misstates a permanent claim about the language's status.

commonMistakes: Letting the plural noun closest to the blank set the verb form instead of the real subject.

whyCorrect: The first part is anchored in 1940, when scientists assumed the hormone existed only in animals. The second reports what scientists know now, that it also occurs in chokecherry plants, and adds that this took decades to discover. The transition has to mark the jump from that past assumption to present knowledge, which Today does.

whyWrong.B: For instance would make the plant finding an example of the animals-only assumption, but it is a counterexample to it.
whyWrong.C: In other words signals a restatement, and the second sentence introduces new and contrary information.
whyWrong.D: Thus claims the plant discovery follows from the 1940 assumption, when it overturns that assumption instead.

whyCorrect: The first sentence credits Chaucer with pioneering literary English. The second backs that up with the strongest available evidence, over 2,000 words first recorded in his manuscripts and a contemporary calling him the first finder of the language. In fact is the transition that introduces a striking confirmation of the claim just made.

whyWrong.A: However announces a complication, but the second sentence supports the first rather than qualifying it.
whyWrong.B: Besides tacks on a side point of lesser weight, while this evidence is the central proof of the claim.
whyWrong.D: On the contrary corrects a statement just denied, and nothing has been denied.

whyCorrect: The clause before the semicolon says the gap between the two editions is extreme even for a compulsive reviser. The clause after gives the sharpest measure of that extremity, critics treating the two editions as separate novels. In fact introduces evidence that pushes the previous claim further.

whyWrong.A: By contrast sets the second clause against the first, but it confirms and intensifies it instead.
whyWrong.C: Nevertheless concedes something despite the previous statement, and the critics' view follows from that statement rather than resisting it.
whyWrong.D: In other words signals a restatement in easier terms, while this clause adds new information about how critics respond.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for an example of a service, so the sentence must name a specific one and attach it to Ixmiquilpan. The notes give exactly one service, water treatment, and C states that Ixmiquilpan is responsible for providing it.

whyWrong.A: This says Ixmiquilpan provides public services but names none, so no example appears.
whyWrong.B: This defines Ixmiquilpan as a governmental region providing services, again without naming a single one.
whyWrong.D: This gives the population figure, which is not a service at all.

whyCorrect: A definition states what the term is and what it accomplishes. B does both, giving the process of assigning geographic coordinates to an image and the purpose of letting mapping software place that image in its real-world location. It uses the two definitional notes and nothing else.

whyWrong.A: This reports who used georeferencing and on what, which is an application rather than a definition.
whyWrong.C: This describes the Puerto Rico project and then circularly says it also used georeferencing, so the term is never defined.
whyWrong.D: This states what the georeferenced photographs are good for, not what georeferencing is.

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing to bring out, the different years. Only D states both dates, 1993 for Secrets of a Sparrow and 2017 for The Crossover, and the but before in 2017 marks the gap between them.

whyWrong.A: This says only that both authors are best sellers, with no dates.
whyWrong.B: This groups the two books together and gives no year for either.
whyWrong.C: This contrasts the two books by genre, children's book against memoir, which is a difference but not the one the goal asks for.

tips: When a goal names a specific point of difference, the answer must contain the actual values being compared.

whyCorrect: Despite sets up a reversal: whatever fills the blank has to be overcome by what follows, which is her finding that she could speak authoritatively about Walter's books. The thing that gets overcome is her doubt about her own command of children's literature as a whole. Hesitancy about her expertise names that doubt and contrasts with speaking authoritatively.

whyWrong.A: Exceptions to her expertise would name gaps in what she knows, but the sentence needs an attitude she holds, and Walter's books are presented as an area of strength rather than an exception.
whyWrong.B: Insight into her expertise makes her the analyst of her own knowledge, which gives despite nothing to reverse.
whyWrong.D: An affinity for her expertise is a positive feeling that would support rather than oppose her speaking with authority.

whyCorrect: Though and instead both mark a break with what came before: most studies looked at people living above sea level, and these researchers looked at people living below it. The blank describes the path that departs from the usual one. Innovative is the only choice that means new or different from established practice.

whyWrong.A: Predictable describes the path the earlier studies took, which is what these researchers avoided.
whyWrong.B: Timeworn means long-established, again describing the standard approach rather than the departure.
whyWrong.D: Idealistic concerns pursuing ideals rather than what is practical, which says nothing about breaking with prior research.

whyCorrect: Wong puts composing in quotation marks because she is stretching the word past its usual sense of putting words down. She has just listed what happens during her apparent procrastination, ideas, phrases, hooks, titles, connections. Her point is that this daydreaming is not a delay before the work but a real stage of it, even though no words appear yet.

whyWrong.A: Nothing suggests self-deception; she is correcting the reader's assumption, not her own.
whyWrong.C: She describes ideas and images surfacing in her own mind, not the collecting of outside sources.
whyWrong.D: Comfort is not the claim; she says the time is productive, and reading something brilliant is only one of the settings in which insight arrives.

whyCorrect: Both examples do the same thing: Tagaq puts Inuit throat singing into electronic music, and Black Belt Eagle Scout combines powwow melodies with rock. Each treats the line between Indigenous music and another genre as one they need not respect. Reject is the word for refusing to be bound by those distinctions.

whyWrong.A: Disguise means to conceal something that is still there, but these artists foreground both traditions rather than hiding the boundary.
whyWrong.C: Replace would require something to put in the distinctions' place, and the sentence names no substitute.
whyWrong.D: Observe means to respect or abide by, which is the opposite of what blending two traditions does.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets the standard the prize honors, the greatest benefit to mankind, and Indeed signals that Synge is an instance of it. He won the Nobel for inventing partition chromatography, which is a step forward for his field. Advancement in is the phrase that names such a step and fits the field of chemistry after it.

whyWrong.A: Exposure to would make chemistry something he was subjected to rather than something his work moved ahead.
whyWrong.C: Dependence on describes what his work relied upon, which is no reason to award a prize for benefiting humanity.
whyWrong.D: Controversy in would mean his work provoked dispute, which conflicts with its being honored as a benefit.

whyCorrect: The passage is framed by two sentences about Darius's own sense of himself: it opens with I felt like a tourist and closes with Maybe I wasn't such a tourist. Everything between them is Babou fussing with his cap, meeting his eye, resting hands on his shoulders and saying he is glad Darius is there. The grandfather's attention is what moves Darius from the first thought to the second.

whyWrong.A: Nobody's interest in travel is at issue; tourist here describes how Darius feels among his own family, not a preference about places.
whyWrong.B: The holiday is the setting, and the passage never says Darius has been anticipating it.
whyWrong.C: No future trip to the United States is mentioned anywhere in the text.

tips: When a short narrative opens and closes with the same phrase, the change between the two is usually the point.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports the 2011 conclusion about ocean acidification and fish behavior. Everything after However is about a weakness in that study: a mean sample of roughly 25 fish, and a later review warning that samples this small invite biased analysis and exaggerated effects. The passage exists to raise that doubt about the earlier findings.

whyWrong.B: The subject is a methodological problem in one study, not any neglected aspect of ocean acidification itself.
whyWrong.C: Clark and colleagues raise a general caution about small samples; they do not argue with Devine's team, and no cause of acidification is disputed.
whyWrong.D: No data on how the fish's behavior has changed over time appear in the passage.

whyCorrect: The researchers' claim is not about how writers cite the time; it is that the pattern reflects a real change in how people lived once electric lighting spread in the late nineteenth century. Support therefore has to show behavior shifting at about the right date. Novels after 1880 mentioning far more activity after 10 p.m. is exactly that, since electric light is what let people stay active well past dark.

whyWrong.A: The comparison is anchored at 1800, decades before electric lighting spread, and 10 a.m. is a daylight hour that lighting would not affect.
whyWrong.B: This contrasts two ways of referring to time, implied against clock phrases, which is a matter of narrative style rather than of when people were awake.
whyWrong.C: Equal frequency for noon and midnight is a static fact with no change over time and so cannot support a claim about a shift.

commonMistakes: Supporting the setup sentence about time references instead of the actual conclusion about changed behavior.

whyCorrect: The passage names two opposing effects: plants absorbing more CO2 pushes the net down, and soil microbes respiring more pushes it up. The conclusion is that earlier snow melt raises net CO2, so support has to weaken the absorption side and strengthen the respiration side. A does both, since drier soil limits plant growth while respiration rates go up.

whyWrong.B: This gives plants a longer absorption period and leaves respiration unchanged, which would lower net CO2 rather than raise it.
whyWrong.C: Suppressed respiration cuts the source of the increase, so this pushes against the conclusion even though it also limits plant growth.
whyWrong.D: Amplifying both effects at once leaves the balance between them undetermined, so it supports no particular direction for net CO2.

tips: When two opposing processes set a net value, a supporting finding must move both of them the same way.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that landscape variation matters and that coarse models miss it. The only way to show a coarse model missing something is for the fine grid and the coarse grid to give different answers. C reports exactly that, with autumn respiration rates coming out lower at 1 square kilometer than at 10.

whyWrong.A: The summer-versus-winter difference appears in both grids, so the resolution changes nothing and the conclusion gains no support.
whyWrong.B: A finding of no correlation in either grid again makes the two resolutions agree, which is the opposite of what the conclusion needs.
whyWrong.D: Identical net CO2 from both grids says the coarser model captured the same result, which undercuts the conclusion; the extra volume of data alone is not evidence about accuracy.

whyCorrect: The two findings differ in the time span they cover, not in their reliability. Henry looked at the three years right after liberalization and found investment up sharply; Levine and Zervos looked across 1976 to 1993 and found no lasting increase. Put together, they describe a rise that appears early and then fades.

whyWrong.A: Neither study compares countries that liberalized with countries that did not, and neither measures consistency.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the passage says how long governments keep such policies in place, and Henry's result shows the gains arrive within three years rather than after them.
whyWrong.C: No expectations held by economists before these studies are ever described, so there is nothing to judge as correct.

commonMistakes: Assuming one study must be wrong when the two actually measure different time horizons.

whyCorrect: The study's aim is to judge which conservation strategies work, and the measure of whether a strategy works is what happens to the population. The passage says these primates are hard to count accurately, so it is hard to tell whether the population is rising, falling, or steady. Without a reliable measure of the outcome, judgments about which strategy succeeded can easily be wrong.

whyWrong.A: The passage identifies the counting problem but offers no new counting method, so nothing suggests other researchers would adopt one.
whyWrong.C: Adding more species would not fix an inability to count the muriquis accurately, and no other species is mentioned.
whyWrong.D: The difficulty described is with measuring results, not with the range of strategies the researchers chose to study.
